lines.text: Record a reading or its uncertainty → scale read by eye: $\pm$ half the smallest division (a burette marked every $\pu{0.1 cm3}$: $\pm \pu{0.05 cm3}$); digital display: $\pm$ one unit in the last digit; write the value to the same decimal place as its uncertainty ({{lesson:7.1}}, {{lesson:7.2}})

How many significant figures in a calculated answer? → multiply or divide: the fewest significant figures in the data; add or subtract: the fewest decimal places; exact numbers don't count, and round only at the end ({{lesson:7.2}})
Uncertainty in a titre, a temperature change or another difference → add the absolute uncertainties, so two burette readings give $\pm 0.05 + 0.05 = \pm \pu{0.10 cm3}$ ({{lesson:7.2}})

Uncertainty in a concentration, $\Delta H$ or another product or quotient → add the percentage uncertainties, then convert the total back to an absolute uncertainty; data-booklet values count as exact ({{lesson:7.2}})
Uncertainty in a quantity raised to a power, such as a squared concentration in a rate expression → multiply its percentage uncertainty by the power ({{lesson:7.2}})

Which percentage? → an accepted or data-booklet value: percentage error, the size of the accepted value on the bottom; a before and after: percentage change, initial value on the bottom; two results of equal status: percentage difference, divided by their mean ({{lesson:7.2}})

Evaluate a result → the accepted value outside the result ± its absolute uncertainty (or a percentage error far above the total percentage uncertainty) means systematic errors are present; results that are precise but not accurate also point to a systematic error, which repeats don't reduce ({{lesson:7.2}})

Is $y$ proportional to $x$? → direct: $\frac{y}{x}$ constant, a straight line through the origin; inverse: $xy$ constant. A straight line that misses the origin is linear, not proportional ({{lesson:7.3}})
Rate from a table → change in quantity divided by the time between two rows, which is an average rate; the rate at one instant is the gradient of a tangent ({{lesson:7.3}}, {{lesson:5.3}})

Temperature change in calorimetry with heat loss → extrapolate the cooling line (the warming line if endothermic) back to the time of mixing; concentration by colorimetry → read the sample's absorbance off a calibration line of standards, interpolating within their range ({{lesson:7.3}}, {{lesson:7.1}})
